why_how.text: Highway speeds leave little time to react, so constant scanning and the right lane choice matter.
Speed control slips after a long fast stretch, so the speedometer needs regular checks.

scenario.text: Nora is on a highway with two lanes each way, cruising in the left lane with no one to pass.

reasoning.text: On two or more lanes each way you stay right except to pass, make room for a merging driver, or set up a legal left turn.

result.text: Nora moves back to the right lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the left lane is fine for steady cruising.

correction.text: The left lane is for passing only, and the shoulder or unpaved edge must never be used for passing.

memory_support.text: Keep right, pass left, never the shoulder.

prompt.text: On a highway with two or more lanes each way and no one to pass, which lane belongs to you?

rationale.text: You leave it only to pass slower traffic, make room for a merging driver, or set up a legal left turn.

narration.text: Welcome to the highway driving chapter. Highways bring higher speeds, more lanes and longer trips, so the habits in this chapter matter. This first lesson covers scanning the road, choosing the right lane on a highway with one lane each way and on a highway with two or more lanes each way, controlling your speed, and knowing which lanes may be used for passing. Later lessons cover passing and blind spots, keeping pace with traffic, entrance and exit ramps, highway hypnosis, and what to do after a breakdown or in an emergency on the highway.

lines.text: Look ahead, to the sides, behind.
Never look away more than a few seconds.
Pull off to study a map.

narration.text: Keep scanning ahead, to the sides and behind you, and never look away from the road for more than a few seconds. At highway speed a car covers a long distance in a few seconds, so a long glance at something inside the car means driving blind across that distance. If you need to study a map, first pull safely off the road. The same scanning habit also helps you spot slow vehicles, merging drivers and hazards early, which gives you time to change lanes or ease off instead of reacting at the last moment. Keep scanning ahead, to the sides and behind, and never look away from the road for more than a few seconds; to study a map, first pull safely off the road.

lines.text: Cross the center line only to pass.
No oncoming traffic near, no solid yellow.

narration.text: On a highway with one lane each way, drive in the right lane. You may cross the center line to pass only when no oncoming vehicle is near and there is no solid yellow line on your side. Crossing the center line puts you in the path of oncoming traffic, so both conditions must be met every time. On this kind of road the right lane is the travel lane, and the left side is used only briefly, for passing. Once the pass is complete, you return to the right lane, following the passing steps taught in the next lesson. On a two-lane highway the right lane is the travel lane and the center line may be crossed to pass, while on four or more lanes you keep right except for passing, merging room or a left turn.

title.text: Two or more lanes each way

lines.text: Leave it to pass, make room or turn left.

narration.text: On a highway with two or more lanes each way, stay in the right lane except to pass slower traffic, to make room for a merging driver, or to set up a legal left turn. The left lane is for passing only. The right lane may be used to pass a vehicle that is turning left. The shoulder or unpaved edge must never be used for passing. So on a multi-lane highway, the right lane is home, and you move left only for one of those reasons, then return to the right once you are done. On a two-lane highway the right lane is the travel lane and the center line may be crossed to pass, while on four or more lanes you keep right except for passing, merging room or a left turn.

lines.text: Two lanes: cross the center line to pass.
Four or more: keep right with exceptions.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners mix up the lane rules for two-lane and multi-lane highways. On a two-lane highway, the right lane is the travel lane and the center line may be crossed to pass, when no oncoming vehicle is near and there is no solid yellow line. On a highway with four or more lanes, you keep right except for passing, making room for a merging driver, or setting up a left turn. Neither kind of road ever lets you pass on the shoulder or the unpaved edge. Identify the road first, then apply its rule. On a highway with two or more lanes each way, stay right except to pass slower traffic, make room for a merging driver, or set up a legal left turn.

lines.text: Two or more lanes each way.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a highway with two lanes each way, the traffic is light, and there is no one ahead to pass. Which lane belongs to you? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the right lane. On a highway with two or more lanes each way, you stay right except to pass slower traffic, to make room for a merging driver, or to set up a legal left turn. The left lane is for passing only, so cruising in it with no one to pass is not what the guide describes. The left lane is for passing only, the right lane may be used to pass a vehicle turning left, and the shoulder or unpaved edge must never be used for passing.

To close: keep scanning ahead, to the sides and behind, never look away for more than a few seconds, and pull off the road to study a map. On one lane each way, drive right and cross the center line only to pass when no oncoming vehicle is near and there is no solid yellow line. On two or more lanes each way, stay right except to pass, make room or turn left. Check your speedometer often and watch the posted limits, especially after leaving a fast road for much slower local streets, and never pass on the shoulder. On a highway with two or more lanes each way, stay right except to pass slower traffic, make room for a merging driver, or set up a legal left turn.

why_how.text: Most passing dangers come from what your mirrors cannot show, so blind spots shape every pass.
Trucks and buses have large blind spots that can hide a whole car.

scenario.text: Ken passes a slower car on a four-lane highway and wants to move back into the right lane.

reasoning.text: He waits until the passed car shows in his rearview mirror, looks over his right shoulder and signals.

result.text: Ken returns to the right lane with room to spare.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the same shoulder check for moving out and moving back.

correction.text: Look over the left shoulder before moving out to pass, and over the right one before moving back in.

memory_support.text: Left shoulder out, right shoulder back.

prompt.text: You are about to move back to the right lane after passing. Which shoulder do you look over?

answer.text: Your right shoulder, after the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror.

rationale.text: The left shoulder look comes before moving out to pass; the right shoulder look comes before moving back in.

narration.text: This lesson covers passing on the highway. You will learn the checks to make before you move out to pass, what a blind spot is and why mirrors are not enough, why you should not ride in another driver's blind spot, and how to move through it quickly when you pass. You will also learn the special danger of truck and bus blind spots, how to signal and make the pass, when it is safe to return to your lane, and what to do when someone else is passing you or when many drivers keep passing you on the right. A blind spot is an area your rearview mirrors cannot show, which is why a glance over the shoulder is needed before changing lanes.

lines.text: Quick look over the left shoulder.

narration.text: Before passing on a four-lane highway, check the left lane with your left mirror and your inside mirror, and take a quick look over your left shoulder. The shoulder look is needed because of blind spots. A blind spot is an area your rearview mirrors cannot show, so a car can sit beside you without appearing in either mirror. Only a glance over the shoulder, before changing lanes, tells you that space is empty. Make the mirror checks first, then the shoulder look, and only then begin to move into the left lane. A blind spot is an area your rearview mirrors cannot show, which is why a glance over the shoulder is needed before changing lanes.

lines.text: Do not ride just behind and to the side.
Speed up or drop back to be seen.

narration.text: Avoid riding just behind and to either side of another vehicle, because that puts you in its driver's blind spot. Speed up or drop back so the driver can see you. When you pass, move through the other driver's blind spot as fast as you can without going over the speed limit. The longer you stay in another driver's blind spot while passing, the longer you risk that vehicle moving into yours. So a good pass is not a slow, side-by-side crawl but a steady, smooth move past the other vehicle within the limit. Avoid riding just behind and to either side of another vehicle; speed up or drop back so its driver can see you.

lines.text: No face in the mirror, no view of you.
Return only when you see the cab.

narration.text: Do not linger beside or right behind a truck or bus. Their large blind spots can hide your car completely. A simple test helps: if you cannot see the trucker's face in the truck's side mirror, the trucker cannot see you. After passing a truck, wait until its cab appears in your rearview mirror before returning to the lane, keep your speed, and do not slow down in front of it. A truck needs far more room to stop than a car, so cutting back in close and slowing is especially dangerous. Do not linger beside or right behind a truck or bus, whose large blind spots hide you; if the trucker's face is not visible in the side mirror, you are not visible to the trucker.

If the way is clear after your mirror and shoulder checks, signal the lane change, then pass quickly and smoothly without exceeding the speed limit. Return to the right lane only once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror, after a look over your right shoulder and a signal. Seeing the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror means you have left it enough room. The signal tells the driver you passed, and anyone behind, that you are moving back. Then settle into the right lane and continue at a steady pace with the flow of traffic.

Here is the trap. The shoulder check flips with the direction of the lane change. Before moving out to pass, you look over your left shoulder, because the space you are moving into is on your left. Before moving back in, you look over your right shoulder, because now the space you are moving into is on your right. Learners who remember only one shoulder check use it both times and miss the side that matters. On a test, match the shoulder to the direction you are moving: left to go out, right to come back in. Return to the right lane only once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror, after a look over your right shoulder and a signal.

Here is a quick check: you have just passed a slower car on a four-lane highway and want to move back into the right lane. Which shoulder do you look over, and what else do you wait for? Work it out before reading on. You look over your right shoulder and signal, but only once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror. The left shoulder look is the one you made before moving out to pass. If the vehicle you passed was a truck, you wait until its cab appears in your mirror and you do not slow down in front of it. After passing a truck, wait until its cab appears in your rearview mirror before returning to the lane, keep your speed, and do not slow down in front of it.

lines.text: Hold your lane; do not speed up.
Many passing on the right? Move right.

narration.text: To close, here is the other side of passing. When someone starts to pass you, hold your lane and do not speed up, because speeding up makes the pass longer and more dangerous. If many drivers are passing you on the right on a multi-lane road, you are likely slower than traffic and should move right when it is clear, unless a left turn is coming up. And when you pass, check your left and inside mirrors and look over your left shoulder, move through blind spots quickly, and return only once the passed vehicle shows in your rearview mirror.

why_how.text: Many crashes happen when one driver is faster or slower than the rest of traffic.
Watching behind and far ahead lets you adjust early instead of braking hard.

scenario.text: Sam drives well under the speed of traffic, and a long line of cars builds up behind him.

reasoning.text: Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous, and the guide says to pull over when safe and let them by.

result.text: Sam pulls over at a safe spot and lets the line pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking speeding saves a lot of time.

correction.text: Speeding saves no more than a few minutes an hour, and each pass adds another chance of a collision.

memory_support.text: Match the flow; look early; never stop in lanes.

prompt.text: A line of vehicles has built up behind your slow car. What should you do?

answer.text: Pull over when it is safe and let them by.

rationale.text: Driving much slower than traffic is dangerous too, so let the line pass at a safe spot rather than holding everyone back.

narration.text: This lesson covers how fast to drive on the highway and how to manage the space around you. You will learn why keeping pace with traffic matters, what speeding really gains, why driving too slowly is also dangerous, how often to check your mirrors, why to spot slow vehicles early, where never to stop, and how looking far ahead helps you avoid panic stops. Together these habits keep you from becoming the car that is out of step with everyone else, which is when many highway crashes happen. Look far enough ahead to avoid panic stops, because hard braking can cost you control and makes it harder for drivers behind to stop.

lines.text: Each pass adds a collision chance.

narration.text: Crashes involving two or more vehicles often happen when one driver goes faster or slower than the others, so keep pace with traffic. Speeding does not pay off: it saves no more than a few minutes an hour, and each pass you make adds another chance of a collision. A driver weaving past others to gain a few minutes takes on many extra risks for very little time. Settling into the flow of traffic, within the speed limit, keeps you predictable to the drivers around you and reduces the number of passes you need to make. Speeding saves no more than a few minutes an hour, and each pass you make adds another chance of a collision.

lines.text: Much slower than traffic is risky.
A line behind you? Pull over safely.

narration.text: Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous. Other drivers come up on a slow car quickly and may brake hard or pass in risky places. If a line of vehicles builds up behind you, pull over when it is safe and let them by. That is not a defeat; it removes the reason for drivers behind you to attempt a dangerous pass. Slow trucks and small underpowered vehicles may lose speed on long or steep climbs and need extra time to get up to speed when they join traffic, so expect them and plan for them. Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous; if a line of vehicles builds behind you, pull over when safe and let them by.

lines.text: Change lanes or ease off early.

narration.text: Check your rearview mirrors every few seconds to track traffic coming up behind you. Spot slow vehicles early, such as heavy trucks and underpowered cars on steep grades or merging onto the highway, so you can change lanes or ease off instead of braking suddenly. Keep a safe following distance from the vehicle ahead, using the spacing method taught in the everyday driving chapter. With mirrors checked often and slow vehicles spotted early, you always know what is around you and have time to make a smooth adjustment rather than a sudden one.

title.text: Never stop in a travel lane

lines.text: Use rest stops and service areas.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When tired, lost or needing a break, some drivers simply stop in a quiet travel lane, thinking traffic will go around. The guide says never stop in the travel lanes of a highway. Use rest stops and service areas instead. A stopped car in a travel lane at highway speeds is one of the most dangerous situations on the road, because drivers coming up behind may not realize it is stopped until too late. If you have a true emergency, the shoulder is the place, as a later lesson explains, not a travel lane. Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous; if a line of vehicles builds behind you, pull over when safe and let them by.

Look far enough ahead to avoid panic stops. Hard braking can cost you control of the car and makes it harder for the drivers behind you to stop. Slowing down or changing lanes early may let you avoid stopping entirely, and any stop you do make will be more gradual and safer. That is the payoff of scanning far down the road: you see a slowdown, a stalled car or a merging truck early enough to ease off smoothly. Drivers behind you see your brake lights in time and can slow down gradually too. Look far enough ahead to avoid panic stops, because hard braking can cost you control and makes it harder for drivers behind to stop.

Here is a quick check: you are driving well under the speed of traffic on a two-lane highway, and a long line of vehicles has built up behind you. What should you do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to pull over when it is safe and let them by. Driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous, because it pushes other drivers into risky passes, and crashes involving two or more vehicles often happen when one driver goes faster or slower than the others. Never stop in a travel lane to let them pass. Never stop in the travel lanes of a highway; use rest stops and service areas instead.

lines.text: Keep pace; never stop in lanes.

narration.text: Let us sum up. Crashes involving two or more vehicles often happen when one driver goes faster or slower than the others, so keep pace with traffic. Speeding saves no more than a few minutes an hour, and each pass adds a chance of collision, while driving much slower than traffic is also dangerous, so pull over and let a line of vehicles by. Check your mirrors every few seconds, spot slow vehicles early, keep a safe following distance, never stop in travel lanes, and look far enough ahead to avoid panic stops. Spot slow vehicles early, such as heavy trucks and underpowered cars on steep grades or merging, so you can change lanes or ease off instead of braking suddenly.

why_how.text: Entering and leaving a highway safely depends on using the ramp lanes the way they are designed.
Interchanges can be confusing, so knowing the common layouts helps first-time drivers.

scenario.text: Ana is on an entrance ramp, and the highway drivers are not making room for her.

reasoning.text: Drivers on the highway should make room, but if they do not, she must yield rather than force her way in, even if that means stopping.

result.text: Ana waits for a gap and then merges.

claim.text: Common mistake: backing up on the shoulder after missing an exit.

correction.text: Never stop, back up or turn around on the highway; take the next exit and come back.

memory_support.text: Speed up to merge, slow down to leave, next exit if missed.

prompt.text: Where on the ramps are the acceleration and deceleration lanes, and what is each used for?

answer.text: The acceleration lane ends most entrance ramps and is for speeding up; the deceleration lane starts most exit ramps and is for slowing down.

rationale.text: You reach highway speed in the acceleration lane before merging, and you slow down in the deceleration lane and on the exit ramp.

narration.text: This lesson covers how you get on and off a highway. You will learn what a controlled access highway is, how entrance and exit ramps work, how to use the acceleration lane to merge, what to do if highway drivers do not make room, how to use the deceleration lane to exit, what to do if you miss your exit, and the common interchange layouts, including the diverging diamond. Ramps and interchanges are where highway traffic meets traffic joining or leaving it, so they call for careful speed control and clear signals. Use the entrance ramp and its acceleration lane to reach the speed of highway traffic, then signal and merge smoothly into a gap.

lines.text: On and off only at ramps.

narration.text: A controlled access highway lets you get on or off only at entrance and exit ramps. There are no driveways or crossroads joining it. Entrance ramps and exit ramps are both short ramps that carry traffic in one direction only, so you never meet oncoming traffic on a ramp. An acceleration lane sits at the end of most entrance ramps and is for speeding up, while a deceleration lane sits at the start of most exit ramps and is for slowing down. Knowing which lane is which helps you plan your speed at both ends of the trip. Entrance ramps and exit ramps are both short ramps that carry traffic in one direction only.

lines.text: Use the ramp to reach traffic speed.
Signal and merge into a gap.
Stop only in very heavy traffic.

narration.text: Use the entrance ramp and its acceleration lane to reach the speed of highway traffic, then signal and merge smoothly into a gap. Merging at highway speed lets you blend in without forcing others to brake. Stopping where the acceleration lane ends is only for very heavy traffic that leaves you no choice. Drivers on the highway should make room for you, but if they do not, you must yield to them rather than force your way in, even if that means stopping. The driver already on the highway is not required to give up the lane.

lines.text: Get into the correct lane early.

narration.text: To leave the highway, move into the correct lane well before the deceleration lane. Then use the deceleration lane and the exit ramp to slow down, obeying the ramp's advisory speed sign. Slowing down in the highway travel lanes before you reach the deceleration lane surprises the drivers behind you, so wait until you are in the deceleration lane to brake. Ramps often curve, which is why they carry an advisory speed. Plan your exit early by watching the signs, so you are in the right lane long before the ramp begins. An acceleration lane sits at the end of most entrance ramps and is for speeding up, while a deceleration lane sits at the start of most exit ramps and is for slowing down.

lines.text: Never back up or turn around.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a driver realizes the exit has just gone by, the urge is to stop, back up along the shoulder, or turn around through the median. The guide says never stop, back up or turn around on the highway. Take the next exit and come back. Backing up or stopping on a highway puts you in the path of traffic moving at full speed, whose drivers will not expect a car going the wrong way or standing still. A missed exit costs a few minutes; an unsafe recovery can cost much more. If you miss your exit, never stop, back up or turn around on the highway; take the next exit and come back.

lines.text: Diverging diamond: briefly on the left.

narration.text: An interchange is where two busy highways meet using entrance and exit ramps, and it can be confusing the first time you use it. The guide pictures four common layouts: the cloverleaf, the diamond, the directional, and the diverging diamond. On a Diverging Diamond Interchange, you drive on the left side of the road for a short stretch before crossing back. Directional signs at every interchange help you find your way, so read them early and get into the lane they point you to before you reach the ramps. The guide pictures four common interchange layouts: cloverleaf, diamond, directional and diverging diamond.

Here is a quick check: where are the acceleration and deceleration lanes found, and what is each one used for? Work it out before reading on. The acceleration lane sits at the end of most entrance ramps and is for speeding up to the speed of highway traffic before you signal and merge into a gap. The deceleration lane sits at the start of most exit ramps and is for slowing down, along with the exit ramp itself, where you obey the advisory speed sign. Speed up to enter, slow down to leave. Move into the correct lane well before the deceleration lane, then use that lane and the exit ramp to slow down, obeying the ramp's advisory speed sign.

To sum up: a controlled access highway is entered and left only at one-way ramps. Use the acceleration lane at the end of the entrance ramp to reach traffic speed, then signal and merge into a gap, yielding if highway drivers do not make room, and stopping at the lane's end only in very heavy traffic. Move into the correct lane early, slow down in the deceleration lane and on the ramp, and obey its advisory speed. If you miss your exit, take the next one. At a diverging diamond you briefly drive on the left. Drivers on the highway should make room for you, but if they do not, you must yield to them rather than force your way in, even if that means stopping.

why_how.text: Long, unchanging highway drives can lull a driver into an unaware state.
Drowsiness slows decisions and reactions, which is dangerous at highway speed.

scenario.text: After three hours on a straight highway, Leo notices he cannot remember the last few miles.

reasoning.text: That drowsy, unaware state is highway hypnosis, and the guide says leave the highway if you start to feel sleepy.

result.text: Leo takes the next exit and rests before continuing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a drowsy driver is much safer than a drunk one.

correction.text: A drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one.

memory_support.text: Eyes moving; sleepy means get off.

prompt.text: What single fix does the guide give for both highway hypnosis and plain sleepiness?

answer.text: Get off the highway rather than risk falling asleep at the wheel.

rationale.text: Keep your eyes moving to prevent hypnosis, and if you still feel sleepy, leave the highway and rest.

narration.text: This lesson covers staying alert on the highway. Long highway drives can be monotonous: the road looks the same, traffic moves steadily, and the sounds of the car blend together. You will learn what highway hypnosis is and what causes it, how to prevent it, why drowsy driving is so dangerous, and the single fix the guide gives for both hypnosis and plain sleepiness. You will also see the guide's reminder that many crashes happen simply because drivers do not give enough attention to driving, so staying alert is a basic safety duty.

lines.text: Steady hum of wind, tires, engine.

narration.text: Highway hypnosis is a drowsy, unaware state caused by the sameness of the road and traffic and the steady hum of wind, tires and engine. A driver in this state may keep the car in the lane yet stop really noticing what is happening, and may not remember the last stretch of road. It creeps up gradually, which is why it is dangerous: the driver does not feel a sudden change. Long, straight highways with little variety are where it is most likely, so they are where you need to watch yourself most closely. Many crashes happen because drivers do not give enough attention to driving, so stay alert for unexpected events.

Prevent highway hypnosis by keeping your eyes moving over traffic and signs, rather than staring at one spot ahead. Moving your eyes keeps your brain engaged with the scene around you. If you start to feel sleepy, leave the highway. A drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one. If you are very sleepy, stop at the nearest rest area or service area and take a nap. Do not try to push through, because the danger grows the longer you keep driving drowsy. Prevent highway hypnosis by keeping your eyes moving over traffic and signs, and leave the highway if you start to feel sleepy.

Here is the trap. Drivers often try home remedies to stay awake behind the wheel and keep going. The guide gives one fix for both highway hypnosis and plain sleepiness: get off the highway rather than risk falling asleep at the wheel. Keeping your eyes moving helps prevent hypnosis, but once you feel sleepy, the answer is to leave the highway and rest, at the nearest rest area or service area if you are very sleepy. On a test, an answer that keeps you driving while sleepy misses the guide's point. A drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one, so stop at the nearest rest area or service area and nap if very sleepy.

Here is a quick check: what single fix does the guide give for both highway hypnosis and plain sleepiness at the wheel? Work it out before reading on. The fix is to get off the highway rather than risk falling asleep at the wheel. To prevent highway hypnosis in the first place, keep your eyes moving over traffic and signs. If you are very sleepy, stop at the nearest rest area or service area and nap, because a drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one. Prevent highway hypnosis by keeping your eyes moving over traffic and signs, and leave the highway if you start to feel sleepy.

To close: highway hypnosis is a drowsy, unaware state caused by the sameness of the road and traffic and the steady hum of wind, tires and engine. Prevent it by keeping your eyes moving over traffic and signs, and leave the highway if you start to feel sleepy. A drowsy driver decides and reacts more slowly and can be as dangerous as a drunk one, so stop at the nearest rest area or service area and nap if very sleepy. Many crashes happen because drivers do not give enough attention to driving, so stay alert for unexpected events.

why_how.text: A stalled car on a highway is dangerous because other drivers may notice it too late.
Getting off the road and signaling trouble protects you while you wait for help.

scenario.text: Mia's car starts to lose power just past the crest of a hill, and the shoulder is narrow.

reasoning.text: She should get off the road if possible, and if she cannot leave the roadway, stop where others can clearly see her, not just past a hill crest.

result.text: Mia coasts to a visible spot, turns on her flashers and raises the hood.

claim.text: Common mistake: changing a flat tire from inside the traffic lane.

correction.text: Never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane.

memory_support.text: Off the road, flashers on, hood up, flares behind.

prompt.text: Your car breaks down and you cannot leave the roadway. Where should you stop?

answer.text: Where others can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve.

rationale.text: Get off the road if at all possible; if not, choose a visible spot and turn on your flashers.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter covers what to do when something goes wrong on the highway. You will learn where you may stop in an emergency and how to signal it, why being seen after a breakdown is so important, how to report a breakdown, where to stop if you cannot leave the roadway, how to use emergency flares, and why you must never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane. You will also learn the places the guide suggests for tying a white cloth to signal that you need help. After a breakdown, make sure other drivers can see you and your vehicle, since crashes happen when a stalled car is noticed too late.

lines.text: Raise the hood or tie a white cloth.

narration.text: In an emergency you may stop on the shoulder. Turn on your emergency flashers, and raising the hood or tying a white cloth to the antenna also helps. These are the signals the guide suggests for an emergency stop on the shoulder: emergency flashers, a raised hood, and a white cloth on the antenna. They tell passing drivers that your car is stopped and that you may need help. The breakdown page adds the side mirror and the door handle as other places to tie the white cloth, beyond the antenna. A white cloth on the antenna and a raised hood are the signals suggested for an emergency stop on the shoulder, together with emergency flashers.

title.text: Be seen, get off the road

lines.text: Crashes happen when stalled cars are seen late.
Get off the road if possible.

narration.text: After a breakdown, make sure other drivers can see you and your vehicle, since crashes happen when a stalled car is noticed too late. With vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if at all possible, and turn on your emergency flashers. Report the breakdown with a two-way radio or a phone. Road signs may list a CB channel or a number to call, and there is a cellphone emergency number. If you cannot leave the roadway, stop where others can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve.

lines.text: Not just past a hill crest.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a car loses power, drivers often stop the moment they can, wherever that is. If you cannot leave the roadway, stop where others can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve. Drivers coming over a crest or around a curve have little time to see a stopped car and react. If the car is still rolling, use that momentum to reach a spot with a long, clear view behind you. On a test, any answer that stops you just past a crest or around a bend is wrong. With vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if at all possible, and turn on your emergency flashers.

lines.text: Never change a tire in a traffic lane.

narration.text: Set emergency flares behind a disabled vehicle to warn drivers to change lanes before they reach it. Never stand in the roadway, and never change a tire from inside a traffic lane, because drivers may not see you until they are very close. Signal trouble by lifting the hood or tying a white cloth to the antenna, the side mirror or a door handle. Those signals let you ask for help from a safe place rather than by standing near traffic. Your safety outside the car matters more than the car itself. The breakdown page adds the side mirror and door handle as places to tie a white cloth, beyond the antenna.

Here is a quick check: your car breaks down on a busy highway, and you cannot get it off the roadway. Where should you stop it? Work it out before reading on. Stop where other drivers can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve. Getting off the road and away from traffic is always the first choice if at all possible. Wherever you stop, turn on your emergency flashers, set flares behind the vehicle, and never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane. Never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane; signal trouble by lifting the hood or tying a white cloth to the antenna, side mirror or door handle.

lines.text: Visible spot, flares, stay out of lanes.

narration.text: To finish the chapter: in an emergency you may stop on the shoulder with your flashers on, and raise the hood or tie a white cloth to the antenna, side mirror or door handle. After a breakdown, make sure you can be seen, get off the road if at all possible, and report it by radio or phone. If you cannot leave the roadway, stop where others can clearly see you, not just past a hill crest or around a curve. Set flares behind the vehicle, and never stand in the roadway or change a tire from inside a traffic lane. After a breakdown, make sure other drivers can see you and your vehicle, since crashes happen when a stalled car is noticed too late.
